title: The Economic Impact of Hurricane Katrina on its Victims: Evidence from Individual Tax Returns
research_question: What were the long-term economic and social consequences of Hurricane Katrina for the people who were living in New Orleans when the storm struck? Specifically, how did the disaster affect victims' wage earnings, employment, total income, unemployment insurance receipt, retirement savings withdrawals, mobility, marriage, divorce, and fertility over the years following the storm, and how did these effects vary with the severity of local property damage, pre-storm income, and age?
data_description: The analysis uses the universe of U.S. federal individual income tax returns filed between 1999 and 2010, housed at the IRS Compliance Data Warehouse. The unit of observation is a tax-filing household-year, tracked by the primary filer. Treated households are all those filing 2004 returns from New Orleans zip codes (about 187,000 households covering roughly 358,000 individuals). Comparison households are drawn as a 10% random sample from ten demographically similar large U.S. cities (e.g., Baltimore, Detroit, Memphis, Newark, St. Louis). Variables include wage and salary income, self-employment (Schedule C) income, unemployment compensation, adjusted gross income, Social Security income, gross retirement account distributions, filing status (used to infer marriage/divorce), number of child dependents, age of primary filer, homeownership proxies, and filing zip code (used to infer mobility). Auxiliary data come from the 2000 Census, 2001–2005 ACS, FEMA flood and zip-code damage classifications, FHFA housing price indices, and BEA REIS data.
institutional_context: Hurricane Katrina made landfall on the Louisiana coast on August 29, 2005, breaching levees around New Orleans and flooding roughly 80% of the city. The storm killed nearly 2,000 people, destroyed more than 200,000 homes, caused over $100 billion in damage, and triggered a massive, largely unanticipated displacement: more than half of New Orleans residents filed their next tax return from a different city, and the city's population remained roughly 25% smaller years later. Damage was geographically uneven; FEMA classified New Orleans zip codes as 'look and leave' (most damaged), 'look and stay,' or unrestricted. Victims received extensive public and private assistance, including over $100 billion in federal disaster relief, expanded unemployment insurance (including Disaster Unemployment Assistance and 13 extra weeks of benefits), an expanded Work Opportunity Tax Credit, a temporary waiver of the early-withdrawal penalty on retirement account distributions for affected residents, and more than $4 billion in charitable donations. This setting provides a sudden, large, and largely exogenous shock to a defined population whose subsequent outcomes can be tracked against residents of comparable cities.
